summary: A LiteLLM proxy in front of whatever your organisation licenses. You give the base URL and the model ids; this fragment already knows how LiteLLM behaves on the wire.

requires.name: {{apiKeyEnv}}
requires.description: The virtual key your LiteLLM proxy issued you (sk-...). It is a key minted by the proxy, not a vendor key: the proxy holds the upstream credentials.
requires.howTo: Ask whoever runs the proxy for a virtual key, or mint one yourself on the LiteLLM admin UI under Virtual Keys. The installer writes it to ~/.pi/secrets.env (chmod 0600) or the macOS Keychain; nothing else needs it.

prompts.label: Full base URL of your LiteLLM proxy, including the /v1 suffix
prompts.help: Absolute http(s). PI appends /chat/completions to it, and the verification one-liners below append /model/info, so give it WITH /v1 — both routes exist under that prefix.

validate.message: an absolute http:// or https:// URL, no trailing spaces

prompts.label: Name of the environment variable that will hold your LiteLLM virtual key
prompts.help: The NAME, not the key. LITELLM_API_KEY is LiteLLM's own convention and is what its docs and CLI use; change it only if your organisation already exports something else.

validate.message: an environment variable name: uppercase letters, digits and underscores

prompts.label: Where does this proxy physically send your prompts?
prompts.help: A fact about YOUR deployment, not about LiteLLM. A proxy your company runs that fans out to a public vendor is still public: the class describes where the bytes end up, not who owns the first hop.

choices.label: public - it forwards to a third-party vendor API
internal - it stays inside your network or your own cloud tenancy
confidential - it serves models running on infrastructure you control end to end

prompts.label: How many requests may this harness have in flight against the proxy at once?
prompts.help: LiteLLM enforces rpm/tpm per virtual key and answers 429 past it. 2 is the safe default for a key you have not measured; raise it once you know your budget.

prompts.label: Model id, exactly as the proxy serves it
prompts.help: The proxy's own public_model_name, which is whatever its operator called it and is usually NOT the vendor's id. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" <baseUrl>/model/info | jq -r '.data[].model_name'` lists them.

prompts.label: Context window for that model - min(200000, what this deployment actually serves)
prompts.help: Read it out of /model/info as .data[].model_info.max_input_tokens. Under-declaring only makes compaction fire earlier, which is safe; over-declaring is what kills turns.

prompts.label: Does that model take a reasoning_effort (is it a thinking model)?
prompts.help: true only if you know it reasons. A false here costs you the thinking menu; a wrong true sends reasoning_effort to a model that does not take one, and unless the proxy runs with drop_params that is a 400 on every turn.

prompts.label: A second model id for the light tier, or blank if you only want one
prompts.help: Worth filling in: the light tier is what summarisation, titles and the cheap dispatch lane use, and pointing it at your strong model multiplies their cost.

prompts.label: Context window for the second model
Does the second model take a reasoning_effort?

notes: ONE FRAGMENT, ONE PROXY. The fragment id is the key this provider gets in config/models.json, so a second LiteLLM deployment cannot be a second answer to this file - it would overwrite the first. Copy litellm.json to litellm-<something>.json, change `id` to match the filename, and select both at install time.

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS NEXT TO openai-compatible.json, WHICH ALSO FITS. Both speak /v1/chat/completions under the endpoint's own model names, so on the interview they differ by two questions and nothing else. The split rests on TWO facts, and both are about LiteLLM the product rather than about anyone's deployment - which matters, because a fact about a deployment is an answer and belongs in a prompt, while a fact about a product can only be a literal: compat, reasoning and thinkingLevelMap may not be deferred to a prompt (README section 2.8 allows exactly egress, concurrency and a requires[].name). (1) The thinkingLevelMap SHAPE below: xhigh and none are opt-in while low and minimal are opt-out, an asymmetry that lives in litellm's own transformation code and has no counterpart in vLLM or OpenRouter. (2) maxTokensField: max_tokens is correct here because LiteLLM TRANSLATES it per upstream provider, and wrong for a direct GPT-5-class endpoint, which requires max_completion_tokens - the same value for the opposite reason, which the generic fragment cannot state. A third leg was proposed and withdrawn: see the supportsUsageInStreaming note, which is right about the flag and was wrong about the mechanism. If your endpoint is a vLLM server, OpenRouter or an in-house router, use openai-compatible - it is still the right answer for everything unnamed.

THE COMPAT FLAGS HERE ARE READ OUT OF THE INSTALLED litellm 1.89.7 WHEEL, NOT PROBED AGAINST YOUR PROXY. That is a weaker claim than the measured tables in databricks.json and github-copilot.json, and it is labelled as such deliberately - but every line below names the file it came from, so you can check it rather than trust it. supportsReasoningEffort: router.py:1877-1883 builds the upstream call as {**litellm_params, ..., **kwargs} with the caller LAST, and llms/openai/chat/gpt_5_transformation.py:171 lists reasoning_effort as a first-class param, so it reaches the upstream transformation rather than being dropped. maxTokensField max_tokens: the same file at :270-275 says in as many words that max_tokens is not supported for gpt-5 models on the OpenAI API and rewrites it to max_completion_tokens for you - which is why the LEGACY field is the right one to send through a proxy and the wrong one to send to that endpoint directly. supportsFinishReason: the proxy returns the OpenAI response schema, finish_reason included; the flag matters because its absence looks like a hung agent rather than an error, so if a turn never ends, flip it to false and PI infers the stop itself. supportsDeveloperRole is left false because it depends on the model behind the id rather than on LiteLLM, and under-declaring costs nothing: the turn is sent with a system message instead. The verify one-liners below turn every one of these from read into measured in about a minute.

supportsUsageInStreaming IS true SO THAT PI ASKS, AND THAT IS ALL IT MEANS. Usage rides in the final streamed chunk only when the request itself carried stream_options.include_usage: litellm_core_utils/streaming_handler.py:174 sets send_stream_usage from check_send_stream_usage(self.stream_options), and that helper (:251) is true only when the client asked. So this flag is what makes PI send stream_options.include_usage, and it is the only way the token counters on the status line get real numbers on a streamed turn. A LiteLLM operator can additionally force it on for every client with general_settings.always_include_stream_usage (proxy/common_request_processing.py:948-961), which is OFF by default and is not something you set from here. NOTE WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is plain OpenAI streaming semantics, equally true of vLLM and OpenRouter, so it is NOT one of the reasons this file is separate from openai-compatible.json - see the note above, which names the two that are. An earlier draft of this note claimed the proxy adds include_usage on its own and then strips the usage block back out; there is no such code in litellm 1.89.7 and the symbol it named does not exist. Read against the installed wheel.

THE thinkingLevelMap IS A DELIBERATE FOUR ENTRIES, AND WHAT IS MISSING MATTERS MORE THAN WHAT IS THERE. xhigh and max are absent, which pi-ai reads as unsupported - correct here, because llms/openai/chat/gpt_5_transformation.py:236-247 makes xhigh an OPT-IN capability ("only allow if model explicitly supports it": supports_xhigh_reasoning_effort must be literally true in that deployment's model_info) and raises UnsupportedParamsError with status 400 when it is not, unless the proxy runs with drop_params. The same file at :249-259 makes minimal and low OPT-OUT - unknown models pass through, and only an explicit false blocks them - and :188 / :279 gate none the same way as xhigh. THAT ASYMMETRY IS THE REASON THIS FILE EXISTS: it is a property of litellm's transformation code, not of your deployment, so it is the same on every LiteLLM proxy and has no counterpart in vLLM or OpenRouter. off is absent too, and absent is NOT the same as null: an absent level stays supported and reaches the wire as no parameter at all, which leaves your endpoint applying ITS OWN DEFAULT EFFORT rather than none, while nulling off would be worse still - PI would clamp a request for off UPWARDS to minimal, clampThinkingLevel walking up before it walks down, and quietly buy more thinking than was asked for. Absent is right here only because the spelling for no reasoning belongs to the endpoint behind the proxy and cannot be known from this file; if yours accepts one, map off to it, and see docs/configuration/models.md for the three states side by side. To enable xhigh once your operator has set the flag, add "xhigh": "xhigh" to that model's map in config/models.json and confirm the flag through /model/info first.

reasoning IS ASKED PER MODEL AND DEFAULTS TO false ON PURPOSE. PI never emits reasoning_effort for a model with `reasoning: false` - every level clamps to off and the emitter writes nothing - so a wrong false only costs you the thinking menu. A wrong true sends the parameter to a model that has no use for it, and a LiteLLM proxy that is not running with drop_params answers 400 on every turn rather than ignoring it. Say true only for ids you know reason.

MODEL IDS ARE THE PROXY'S NAMES, NOT THE VENDOR'S. `model_name` in the operator's config.yaml is an alias they chose; the vendor id lives underneath in litellm_params and you never send it. Do not copy ids from a vendor's documentation, and do not copy the examples in this file - they are illustrative. One call lists everything you need for this interview at once: `curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_API_KEY" "<baseUrl>/model/info" | jq -r '.data[] | [.model_name, .model_info.max_input_tokens, .model_info.input_cost_per_token, .model_info.output_cost_per_token] | @tsv'`.

A ZERO ON THE STATUS LINE MEANS UNPRICED, NOT FREE, AND HERE IT IS FIXABLE. `cost` is optional in this file and required on PI's runtime model type, so the composer substitutes {input:0,output:0,cacheRead:0,cacheWrite:0} and every session shows a flat 0.000 while really costing money. It is left out rather than guessed because the price behind a proxy is whatever that deployment's operator configured, not the vendor's list price. To fix it, read input_cost_per_token / output_cost_per_token from /model/info and MULTIPLY BY 1000000: LiteLLM quotes DOLLARS PER TOKEN, PI's `cost` is DOLLARS PER MILLION TOKENS and divides by 1000000 before multiplying by the usage counter, so a per-token figure pasted straight in is wrong by six orders of magnitude and still renders. Add `"cost": {"input": …, "output": …, "cacheRead": 0, "cacheWrite": 0}` next to the model in config/models.json.

TWO FLAGS DELIBERATELY LEFT UNSET. supportsStrictMode - whether strict JSON-schema tool calling survives depends on the model behind the alias, and declaring it wrongly turns occasional malformed tool JSON into a hard rejection. cacheControlFormat - a proxy in the path does not reliably surface cache_control breakpoints, and declaring "anthropic" here would report prompt-cache savings that did not happen.

A 429 IS YOUR KEY'S BUDGET, NOT AN OUTAGE. LiteLLM enforces rpm/tpm and max_budget per virtual key. If turns start failing under load, lower the concurrency answer above or ask for a larger budget - retrying harder makes it worse. There is no failover in this harness: a request to this provider that cannot be served aborts and names it.

verify.label: the proxy answers, and these are the ids it will serve you
your declared context window matches what the deployment reports
reasoning_effort is accepted (only meaningful if you answered true above)
PI can complete one turn on the strong model
